---
title: "Examining named entities against domain text"
subtitle: "Examine correct and incorrect NER outputs"
description: "Learn how spaCy labels named entities in Riverton text and why fictional local names can produce errors."
categories: [phrases and entities, named entity recognition, workforce research]
---

Names in the Riverton job-board and flyer text need labels, not just highlights.
The coordinator wants to know whether a span names an organisation, a date, a
time, a quantity, or something else.

A trained named-entity model can supply those labels quickly.
The team examines its labels for local names absent from the training examples.

::: {.callout-note}
The author created the fictional Riverton Workforce Lab, its job board, and
its training flyer for teaching.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- describe named entity recognition in plain language.
- run spaCy's small English pipeline through spacyr.
- read spaCy entity labels such as PERSON, ORG, DATE, TIME, QUANTITY, and GPE.
- examine entity spans from the 28 Riverton text units.
- explain why fictional local names need checks in context.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Run the released pipeline

The setup chunk reads the sentences, runs the released spaCy pipeline, and
formats entity spans for inspection. **Named entity recognition**, or **NER**,
finds names and assigns each one a type.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(stringr)
library(spacyr)
source("R/use-spacy.R")

sentences <- read_csv(
  "data/workforce/workforce_sentences.csv",
  na = character(),
  col_types = cols(
    sentence_id = col_character(),
    document_id = col_character(),
    source_line = col_character(),
    text = col_character(),
    reference_label = col_character(),
    uncertainty = col_character(),
    annotator_id = col_character(),
    rationale = col_character(),
    codebook_version = col_character(),
    codebook_hash = col_character(),
    derived = col_character(),
    transformation = col_character()
  )
)

pipeline <- use_project_spacy()
pipeline_info <- spacy_pipeline_version()
parsed <- spacy_parse(
  setNames(sentences$text, sentences$sentence_id),
  pos = TRUE,
  lemma = TRUE,
  entity = TRUE,
  dependency = TRUE,
  nounphrase = TRUE
)
entities <- entity_extract(parsed, type = "all") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    sentence_id = doc_id,
    entity = str_replace_all(entity, "_", " "),
    entity_type
  )

example_text <- "Riverton Skills Centre will run evening classes in October."
example_parsed <- spacy_parse(
  c(example = example_text),
  pos = TRUE,
  lemma = TRUE,
  entity = TRUE,
  dependency = TRUE,
  nounphrase = TRUE
)
example_entities <- entity_extract(example_parsed, type = "all") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    entity = str_replace_all(entity, "_", " "),
    predicted_type = entity_type,
    actual_type = c("ORG", "TIME", "DATE"),
    correct = predicted_type == actual_type
  )

title_case_heading <- "Riverton Skills Open House"
title_case_parsed <- spacy_parse(
  c(title_case = title_case_heading),
  pos = TRUE,
  lemma = TRUE,
  entity = TRUE,
  dependency = TRUE,
  nounphrase = TRUE
)
title_case_entities <- entity_extract(title_case_parsed, type = "all") |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    entity = str_replace_all(entity, "_", " "),
    entity_type
  )

spacy_finalize()

pipeline_table <- tibble(
  field = names(pipeline_info),
  value = unlist(pipeline_info, use.names = FALSE)
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  pipeline_table,
  col.names = c("Pipeline field", "Value"),
  caption = "spaCy pipeline used for named entity recognition",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  example_entities,
  col.names = c("Entity", "Predicted type", "Actual type", "Correct"),
  caption = "NER output for a Riverton Skills Centre check sentence",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  title_case_entities,
  col.names = c("Entity", "Entity type"),
  caption = "spaCy output for a title-case version of the flyer heading",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(all(
  c("readr", "dplyr", "tibble", "stringr", "spacyr") %in%
    loadedNamespaces()
))

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(sentences), 28L),
  identical(pipeline$model, "en_core_web_sm"),
  identical(pipeline_info$version, "3.8.0"),
  identical(pipeline_info$license, "MIT"),
  identical(pipeline_info$spacy, "3.8.7"),
  identical(nrow(parsed), 179L),
  identical(example_entities$entity, c("Riverton Skills Centre", "evening", "October")),
  identical(example_entities$predicted_type, c("PERSON", "TIME", "DATE")),
  identical(example_entities$correct, c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE)),
  identical(title_case_entities$entity, "Riverton Skills Open House"),
  identical(title_case_entities$entity_type, "PERSON")
)
```

spaCy incorrectly labels `Riverton Skills Centre` as `PERSON` in the check
sentence. The name refers to the provider, so the hand-assigned label is
`ORG`. A facility interpretation would instead suggest `FAC`.
The fictional name explains the domain mismatch but does not make the output
correct. The title-case heading produces one `PERSON` span.
This shows that surface form can change model output.

## Read the labels

These type names come from the OntoNotes annotation project.
The categories follow that project's conventions.

- `PERSON` means a person.
- `ORG` covers organisations such as companies, agencies, and institutions.
- `DATE` covers dates and periods such as months or years.
- `TIME` marks a time of day or similar expression.
- `QUANTITY` marks an amount with a unit.
- `GPE` covers geopolitical places such as cities, states, and countries.

Context affects the label.
In `Riverton raised the training budget`, `Riverton` can be a `GPE`.
In `Riverton Skills Centre`, it can be part of an `ORG`.

```{r}
entity_type_counts <- entities |>
  count(entity_type, name = "entities", sort = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  entity_type_counts,
  col.names = c("Entity type", "Entities"),
  caption = "Entity types returned for the 28 Riverton text units",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(entities), 10L),
  identical(entity_type_counts$entity_type, c("DATE", "TIME", "ORG", "QUANTITY")),
  identical(entity_type_counts$entities, c(6L, 2L, 1L, 1L)),
  !any(entities$entity_type %in% c("CARDINAL", "GPE")),
  identical(entities$entity[entities$sentence_id == "s023"], "HOUSE")
)
```

The model finds 10 entity spans in the 28 text units.
Six are `DATE`, two are `TIME`, one is `ORG`, and one is `QUANTITY`.
It returns no separate entity for `RIVERTON` in the all-capital heading.
That is defensible because `RIVERTON` belongs to the event name rather than
referring to the town.

The error concerns `HOUSE`. The model selects one word from a four-word event
heading and labels it as an organisation. Both the span and type are wrong.

## Examine the Riverton entities

The table gives hand-assigned labels for the returned spans.
These teaching judgments cover 28 text units, not a public benchmark.

```{r}
entity_answers <- tibble(
  sentence_id = c("s001", "s003", "s008", "s010", "s011", "s014", "s019", "s020", "s023", "s028"),
  entity = c("12 - week", "Evening", "50 pounds", "Six months", "two days", "daytime", "Two years", "Weekend", "HOUSE", "October 15"),
  expected_span = c("12 - week", "Evening", "50 pounds", "Six months", "two days", "daytime", "Two years", "Weekend", "RIVERTON SKILLS OPEN HOUSE", "October 15"),
  expected_type = c("DATE", "TIME", "QUANTITY", "DATE", "DATE", "TIME", "DATE", "DATE", "EVENT", "DATE"),
  note = c(
    rep("The span and type fit this sentence.", 8),
    "The event heading is four words; `HOUSE` alone is the wrong span and `ORG` is the wrong type.",
    "The span and type fit this sentence."
  )
)

entity_judgments <- entities |>
  left_join(entity_answers, by = c("sentence_id", "entity")) |>
  mutate(
    correct = entity == expected_span & entity_type == expected_type
  )

entity_score <- entity_judgments |>
  summarise(
    returned_spans = n(),
    correct_spans = sum(correct),
    wrong_spans = sum(!correct),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  entity_judgments,
  col.names = c("Sentence ID", "Entity", "Predicted type", "Expected span", "Expected type", "Note", "Correct"),
  caption = "Hand check of all spaCy entity spans returned from the 28 text units",
  row.names = FALSE
)

knitr::kable(
  entity_score,
  col.names = c("Returned spans", "Correct spans", "Wrong spans"),
  caption = "Hand-check counts for returned entity spans",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(entity_score$returned_spans, 10L),
  identical(entity_score$correct_spans, 9L),
  identical(entity_score$wrong_spans, 1L),
  !any(is.na(entity_judgments$expected_type)),
  identical(entity_judgments$correct[entity_judgments$sentence_id == "s023"], FALSE),
  identical(entity_judgments$expected_type[entity_judgments$sentence_id == "s023"], "EVENT"),
  identical(entity_judgments$expected_type[entity_judgments$sentence_id == "s028"], "DATE")
)
```

Nine of the ten returned spans match the hand judgments.
This is not a general model evaluation.
Eight correct spans are dates, durations, or times of day.
The ninth is a weight. The only organisation-like output is wrong.

A single score conceals those differences between types.
The check also says nothing about names that the model misses.

## Keep domain mismatch visible

spaCy `en_core_web_sm` 3.8.0 is a released production pipeline.
The author invented the Riverton names for this lesson.
The model cannot assume those names occur in its training data.
It must generalise from surface cues, word shape, and context.
This illustrates domain mismatch, not proof of generally weak performance.

## What to remember

- NER labels spans under an annotation scheme such as OntoNotes.
- The spaCy run returned 10 entity spans from the 28 Riverton text units.
- Ten returned spans are too few, and too uneven by type, to evaluate a model.
- Examine fictional local names directly because domain mismatch can change outputs.

For Riverton work, use NER to collect candidates.
Examine the local names. Report the model version beside the examples.
